title: Grüß's mental-arithmetic cipher
origin: Cipher designed by the mental calculator Wenzel Grüß, published by Klaus Schmeh on 16 October 2026
size: 31 digits in two lines, hiding one German word of exactly ten letters
full_solution: The ten-letter German word together with the method that turns the 31 digits into it.

verification.how: The author fixed the solution in advance by publishing a SHA-256 hash of his solution statement, and confirms a correct answer.

notes: The method can be carried out entirely in the head, for enciphering and deciphering.
The author offers 100 euros to the first person who sends the word and a comprehensible description of how it was found.
A word that is only guessed or matched against the hash, without the method, is not a solution.

author_hints.where: Comments under the challenge post. Some are replies the author gave on Facebook, which a reader quoted there.

hints.hint: The two lines form a single 31-digit number. It is printed in two lines only to make it easier to read.
hints.given: Author's reply on Facebook, quoted by a reader in a comment of 28 October 2026

hints.hint: No special knowledge is required. The author said this in reply to a reader who thought the perfect number 496 was involved.
hints.given: Author's reply on Facebook, quoted by a reader in a comment of 28 October 2026

hints.hint: No mathematical acrobatics are needed. An ambitious seventh-grade pupil who has practised the method should be able to encipher and decipher with it.
hints.given: Author's comments of 31 October and 5 November 2026

hints.hint: A roundabout hint: 'Pickende Hühner' (German for 'pecking chickens').
hints.given: Author's hint on Facebook, quoted by a reader in a comment of 28 October 2026

hints.hint: Asked whether the hint 'Pickende Hühner' refers to the method and not to the solution word, the author answered: the solution word.
Asked whether the letters are first turned into their positions in the alphabet (A = 1 to Z = 26), the author answered: no.
Asked whether the number is built piece by piece, a few digits for each letter, and not by one large calculation, the author answered: piece by piece.
Asked whether the enciphering of a letter depends on earlier letters or digits, the author answered: no.
Asked whether the first digit, 3, belongs to the enciphered content, the author answered: no.
